title: Immunological response to wheat and barley gluten and hydrolyzed barley gluten in patients with celiac disease in remission: a controlled provocation study
summary:
Celiac disease is a chronic, immunologically mediated intestinal disease that is triggered by the intake of gluten in the diet. 
The aim of the study is to better understand how different types of gluten affect the immune system of patients with coeliac disease - especially those who are already on a gluten-free diet and are symptom-free.Gluten is a component of certain grains such as wheat, barley and rye and can trigger a strong immune response in people with coeliac disease. Hydrolyzed or fermented gluten, which is sometimes found in products considered gluten-free, could also cause reactions in rare cases. In this study, we want to test which types of gluten (and in what dosage) might trigger an immune reaction, even if they are contained in processed or gluten-free foods.

The test subjects will receive a total of five test drinks at intervals of 1-2 weeks. These contain various gluten preparations (see below). The amount of gluten administered is low and amounts to a maximum of 5-10% of the normal daily gluten consumption. The test drinks consist of 0.2 liters (1 small glass) of lactose-free chocolate milk/milk substitute or, in the case of cow's milk intolerance, e.g. almond milk:
- Wheat gluten (1000 mg)
- Barley gluten (1000 mg)
- Barley gluten (50 mg)
- Hydrolyzed barley gluten (50 mg)
- Placebo

The order of the gluten samples is determined randomly.
The following tests are carried out before and four hours after each test drink
- Blood sample (three tubes of blood, 3-8 ml each)
- Urine sample.
- Two questionnaires to record symptoms

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- BMI 17-30 kg/m2
- Willingness to participate in the study and signing of the written informed consent form
- Diagnosis of celiac disease according to established guidelines based on positive serology (endomysium test, IgA (in case of IgA deficiency igG) anti-TG2 and/or IgG-DGP) and/or duodenal endoscopy with biopsies showing villous atrophy with Marsh grade >2 according to European guidelines
- Strict adherence to a gluten-free diet in the last 12 months
- Current remission of clinical symptoms
Exclusion criteria:
- Positive serology (IgA anti-TG2) above the upper normal range) at the screening visit
- Existing pregnancy
- Patients with other active inflammatory diseases such as uncontrolled hypo- or hyperthyroidism, type 1 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, kidney disease, inflammatory bowel disease or severe food allergies
- Long-term medication with immunosuppressants/corticosteroids
- Severe acute infection
